column1: RLS security predicates are implemented as {{c1::inline table-valued functions}}.
column2:
They return tables rather than scalar Boolean values.
Review source

column1: An RLS predicate using SELECT 1 WHERE returns {{c1::no rows}} when its access condition is not TRUE.
column2:
A qualifying row represents allowed access rather than a scalar 1 or 0 return value.
Review source

column1: Use WITH {{c1::SCHEMABINDING}} to schema-bind an RLS predicate function.
column2:
The function is an inline TVF returning qualifying rows.
Review source

column1: RLS {{c1::filter predicates}} silently exclude rows that fail their access condition.
column2:
The filtering affects SELECT, UPDATE, and DELETE.
Review source

column1: SQL Server RLS {{c1::block predicates}} raise an error for prohibited writes.
column2:
They enforce write restrictions rather than silently hiding rows.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, filter predicates alone do not validate new {{c1::INSERT}} values.
column2:
An inserted row can become invisible to its creator.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, an {{c1::AFTER INSERT}} block predicate validates newly inserted rows.
column2:
Use it to reject inserted values that violate the access rule.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, an AFTER UPDATE block predicate checks {{c1::new row values}} when its referenced columns change.
column2:
It can prevent changing a visible row into one that violates the tenant rule.
Review source

column1: SQL Server uses {{c1::BEFORE DELETE}} as the block-predicate timing for checking rows before deletion.
column2:
A violation raises an error.
Review source

column1: Set a tenant context with EXEC sys.{{c1::sp_set_session_context}} @key=N'TenantID', @value=42;
column2:
Trusted code must choose the value from the authenticated user's authorized tenant.
Review source

column1: Read a session's TenantID value with {{c1::SESSION_CONTEXT}}(N'TenantID').
column2:
The function returns NULL when the key has no value set.
Review source

column1: SESSION_CONTEXT returns {{c1::sql_variant}} before any explicit conversion to an integer tenant ID.
column2:
The cast makes the expected tenant-identifier type explicit.
Review source

column1: Set {{c1::@read_only}} = 1 to prevent changing a session-context key again on its logical connection.
column2:
Locking the value does not prove that the initial tenant value was authorized.
Review source

column1: Retrieve the current database user's principal ID with {{c1::DATABASE_PRINCIPAL_ID}}().
column2:
An application employee ID is not automatically the same identifier.
Review source

column1: Test current-user membership in SalesManagers with {{c1::IS_MEMBER}}('SalesManagers') = 1.
column2:
An OR branch allowing this role qualifies all rows evaluated by that predicate.
Review source

column1: Create the object that binds RLS predicates to tables with {{c1::CREATE SECURITY POLICY}}.
column2:
The policy identifies predicate functions, target tables, and applicable operations.
Review source

column1: Explicitly enable an RLS policy with WITH (STATE = {{c1::ON}}).
column2:
An enabled policy enforces its configured predicates.
Review source

column1: Protect both Orders and OrderDetails by adding a predicate binding for {{c1::each table}}.
column2:
One policy can reuse the same predicate function for both bindings.
Review source

column1: A {{c1::recursive common table expression (CTE)}} can traverse successive employee-to-manager relationships for hierarchy-based row access.
column2:
The recursive member finds employees whose manager is already in the hierarchy.
Review source

column1: A hierarchy seeded with the current employee and expanded through their reports includes {{c1::that employee and all descendants}}.
column2:
The seed includes the employee's own records as well as subordinate-owned records.
Review source

column1: Disable a policy with ALTER SECURITY POLICY Security.TenantSecurityPolicy WITH (STATE = {{c1::OFF}});
column2:
This stops that policy's row protections, so disabling it can expose previously filtered rows.
Review source

column1: Extend an existing policy with ALTER SECURITY POLICY Security.TenantSecurityPolicy {{c1::ADD FILTER PREDICATE}} Security.fn_TenantAccessPredicate(TenantID) ON dbo.Shipments;
column2:
This binds a filter to another target table.
Review source

column1: Remove Orders' filter binding with ALTER SECURITY POLICY Security.TenantSecurityPolicy {{c1::DROP FILTER PREDICATE}} ON dbo.Orders;
column2:
The policy itself remains in the database.
Review source

column1: Inspect RLS policies and their is_enabled state through {{c1::sys.security_policies}}.
column2:
The enabled-state value is 1 for enabled and 0 for disabled.
Review source

column1: Inspect predicate definitions and target_object_id through {{c1::sys.security_predicates}}.
column2:
Its object_id identifies the containing security policy.
Review source

column1: Enabled RLS on a base table also applies through {{c1::views and stored procedures}} that query it.
column2:
Evaluation uses the effective execution context.
Review source

column1: An enabled SQL Server RLS policy does not automatically exempt {{c1::dbo}}.
column2:
Privileged users can change policies, but their queries do not receive an automatic predicate bypass.
Review source

column1: Reading an RLS-protected table still requires {{c1::SELECT}} permission on the requested data.
column2:
RLS restricts rows but does not grant the underlying read access.
Review source
